item.content:encoded:
Russia–US talks: no breakthrough, no concessions

发布源: 19. Center for Eastern Studies (OSW) --Poland | 抓取时间: 2026-10-24

On 21 October, Vladimir Putin held three hours of talks in St Petersburg with Steve Witkoff, President Donald Trump’s special envoy. The meeting was also attended by Putin’s foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov and the Russian laeader’s special envoy for international investment cooperation Kirill Dmitriev. Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner joined the meeting remotely.

According to the Kremlin spokesman, the talks were substantive, but no arrangements were made for further meetings. Witkoff briefed Putin on his talks in Oslo with the presidents of Ukraine and Finland and the Norwegian prime minister, which he described as constructive. He also presented written proposals outlining elements of a potential peace agreement between Russia and Ukraine. In addition, Witkoff conveyed President Trump’s thanks for the release of US citizen Stephen Hubbard, who had been sentenced to seven years in prison in Russia on charges of allegedly serving as a mercenary for Ukraine. Trump also expressed his gratitude for lifting the ban on diesel exports and the resumption of supplies to the US market.

Putin expressed his willingness to resume trilateral talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US, as proposed by Witkoff, but insisted that they should not begin before mid-November. He also sought to limit their scope to ‘building a security framework for Russia and Ukraine after the conflict ends’. On 14 October, General Andriy Biletsky, commander of the Centre Group, summarised the ‘fourth phase’ of Operation ‘Vivaldi’ being carried out in this area: according to his statement, the Armed Forces of Ukraine (AFU) have liberated approximately 277 km² of territory, neutralising 8,000 enemy soldiers.

Claims by the Russian Ministry of Defence that it has captured Dobropillia are false; however, the situation for the defenders there is deteriorating.Russian forces have significantly intensified their infiltration operations, whilst concentrating troops on the outskirts and in the peripheral districts of the town to prepare for an assault on the centre of Dobropillia. However, the situation for Ukrainian forces on the Orikhiv front has improved following the arrival of substantial reinforcements in the form of the 7th Airborne Assault Corps, redeployed from the Dobropillia sector. The defenders cleared most of Orikhiv of Russian infiltration groups and regained control of the southwestern part of Mala Tokmachka.

item.content:encoded:
Romania’s new government: crisis over, uncertainty ahead

发布源: 19. Center for Eastern Studies (OSW) --Poland | 抓取时间: 2026-10-24

On 20 October, the Romanian parliament approved the government led by Luca Niculescu, a non-partisan diplomat, in a vote of confidence (see Appendix). The cabinet secured 280 votes in favour and 58 against, exceeding the required threshold of 233. It was backed primarily by the post-communist, centre-left Social Democratic Party (PSD), the centre-right National Liberal Party (PNL) and the Democratic Alliance of Hungarians in Romania (UDMR), which represents the Hungarian minority. It also received support from the parliamentary group representing national minorities and some other MPs. The centre-right Save Romania Union (USR) and the pro-Russian SOS Romania voted against the government, while the Eurosceptic, national-conservative Alliance for the Union of Romanians (AUR) boycotted the vote. The new cabinet consists of PSD politicians and non-partisan technocrats nominated by President Nicușor Dan. The PSD controls 11 of the 16 ministries and holds one of the two posts of minister-delegate (without portfolio). Neither the PNL nor the UDMR has joined the government. Instead, both parties have opted to sit in opposition and support government proposals on a case-by-case basis.

The Niculescu government lacks a stable parliamentary majority and will therefore face persistent political uncertainty. Pulaski Commentaries are short analysis of current international developments. The publications are focused on economic and political issues, foreign policy and international security.

Published: October 7, 2026

On 22nd September, in her speech at the United Nations General Assembly (UN GA) the Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi - as the first Japanese leader since 2005 - urged the removal of the ‘enemy state’ clause from the UN Charter. The provision was included in the UN's founding document to denote nations that fought against the Charter’s original signatories during World War II, specifically targeting Axis powers such as Germany, Italy and Japan. Although over eight decades have passed since the end of the conflict and the ‘enemy states’ are well-functioning democracies, the clause remains in its original form. Moreover, in 1995 the UN GA adopted a resolution stipulating it had ‘become obsolete’ and called for its erasure from the Charter.

According to Finnish media reports, the United Kingdom has proposed extending a nuclear umbrella over the members of the Joint Expeditionary Force (JEF). Apart from France and the United States, the UK is the only NATO member possessing its own nuclear capability. The initiative arose in response to declining faith in the nuclear umbrella provided by the United States. Poland's participation in the format would make sense if it were covered by the initiative's nuclear deterrence.

item.content:encoded:
Defence and International Security

发布源: 36. Casimir Pulaski Foundation --Poland | 抓取时间: 2026-10-24

The Pulaski Foundation Defence and Security Program provides multidisciplinary analysis of the current and emerging defense and security challenges facing the Transatlantic Alliance – with a special focus on Central and Eastern Europe.

Since 2022 the program allocates much of its resources to analysing the possible outcomes and consequences for European security of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine. A special component of the program is devoted to the challenges and opportunities facing Poland’s defense policy, including modernizing of the Polish army and its industry. The main goal is to present actionable recommendations to an array of Polish stakeholders, including public administration, which could form a basis for long-term strategies for Poland in times of raising military and defense demands.

Overall, through its analysis, the program advocates for a stronger presence of NATO on the Alliance’s Eastern Flank, more developed European defence capabilities and argues for the need to provide military assistance and solid security guarantees to Ukraine.
